title: C++
description: Write modern C++20 from your very first program: types, functions, references, containers, classes, lambdas and safe memory with unique_ptr. The 80/20 foundation for game and engine code.
keyIdeas: C++ is compiled: the compiler checks every type before anything runs, so fix the first error first and treat warnings as bugs.
Integer maths stays integer (`7 / 2` is 3), and signed overflow, uninitialised variables and out-of-range `[]` are undefined behaviour.
Arguments are copied: take `T&` to change the caller's object and `const T&` to read big objects without copying.
`std::vector` for sequences, `std::array` for fixed sizes, `std::unordered_map` for lookup by key; use `.at()` and `contains` to stay safe.
Classes bundle data with the member functions that protect its rules, and `enum class` and `std::optional` make states and missing values explicit.
Don't write `delete`: objects clean up in their destructors, and `std::unique_ptr` gives each heap object one owner that frees it automatically (RAII).

concepts.label: Compiling and linking
concepts.summary: The compiler checks every file and turns it into machine code, then the linker joins the pieces into an executable; nothing runs until both succeed.

concepts.label: Static types
concepts.summary: Every variable has one type fixed before the program runs, written out or deduced with auto, so the compiler rejects mismatches.

concepts.label: Undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: Operations like reading an uninitialised variable, signed overflow, out-of-range [] or a null dereference have no defined result, so anything can happen.

concepts.label: Integer division
concepts.summary: Dividing two integers drops the fraction (7 / 2 is 3); convert one operand with static_cast<double> for real division.

concepts.label: Integer overflow
concepts.summary: Integers have fixed sizes: signed overflow is undefined behaviour, while unsigned values wrap around.

concepts.label: Conditions and loops
concepts.summary: if/else if runs the first true branch, while and for repeat while a condition holds, and == compares while = assigns.

concepts.label: Functions
concepts.summary: A function has typed parameters and a return type, and must be declared before the code that calls it.

concepts.label: Overloading
concepts.summary: Functions can share a name when their parameters differ; the compiler picks the best match for the argument types, and default arguments fill in missing ones.

concepts.label: References
concepts.summary: A reference (T&) is another name for an existing object, so a reference parameter lets a function change the caller's variable.

concepts.label: const references
concepts.summary: A const T& parameter reads a large object without copying it, and the compiler forbids changing it.

concepts.label: std::vector
concepts.summary: A growable array stored contiguously, and the default container; std::array is its fixed-size cousin.

concepts.label: Range-for loops
concepts.summary: for (T x : v) visits every element: a plain variable is a copy, T& changes the element, const auto& reads without copying.

concepts.label: .at() vs []
concepts.summary: v[i] is unchecked and out-of-range access is undefined behaviour, while v.at(i) throws std::out_of_range.

concepts.label: std::unordered_map
concepts.summary: A hash table from keys to values; m[key] inserts missing keys, so check with contains and read with at.

concepts.label: Pointers
concepts.summary: A pointer holds an address: & takes it, * and -> follow it, and nullptr means it points nowhere.

concepts.label: Structs and classes
concepts.summary: Types that bundle data with member functions; constructors set them up and private members protect their rules (encapsulation).

concepts.label: enum class
concepts.summary: A scoped type with a fixed set of named values that never converts to int, usually handled with a switch.

concepts.label: std::optional
concepts.summary: Holds either a value or nothing (std::nullopt), replacing magic values; read it with value_or or after checking it.

concepts.label: Headers and sources
concepts.summary: Headers declare what exists and are included where needed; .cpp files hold the definitions, compiled separately and linked.

concepts.label: Lambdas
concepts.summary: Inline anonymous functions whose capture list says which local variables they copy or refer to.

concepts.label: Standard algorithms
concepts.summary: Ready-made loops from <algorithm>, such as sort, find_if and count_if, that work on iterator ranges and take lambdas.

concepts.label: Templates
concepts.summary: Code written for a type parameter T, which the compiler turns into a real version for each type used.

concepts.label: Stack vs heap
concepts.summary: Locals live on the stack and are destroyed at the end of their scope; heap objects from new live until something deletes them.

concepts.label: unique_ptr and RAII
concepts.summary: std::unique_ptr owns one heap object and deletes it when it goes out of scope, so cleanup happens on every path.

units.title: First programs
units.description: Compile and run, types, integer maths, decisions, loops and functions.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.takeaway: C++ is compiled: the compiler checks the whole program and builds an executable before anything runs, so read its first error first.

steps.title: From text to a running program

steps.prompt: Put the journey from source file to running program in order.
items: The compiler checks the code and stops with an error if a rule is broken
The compiler translates the code into machine code (an object file)
The linker joins it with library code, such as `std::cout`, into an executable
steps.explanation: Nothing runs until the whole file has passed the compiler's checks and been linked into an executable. That's the big difference from Python, which reads and runs a script line by line: in C++ a typo on line 300 stops the build before line 1 ever runs.

steps.prompt: What does this print? Watch where the `"\n"`s are.
steps.explanation: `3 + 4` is worked out first, so the first line is `Score: 7`. The second statement prints `Lives: 3` **without** a newline, so the next `std::cout` carries on on the same line and adds `!`. Output only moves to a new line when you send `"\n"`.

steps.title: When the compiler says no
steps.body:
If the code breaks a rule, the compiler prints an **error** and no program is built. Each message starts with where it happened, *file:line:column*:

```
hello.cpp:2:9: error: cannot initialize a variable of type 'int' with an lvalue of type 'const char[5]'
```

- Fix the **first** error first: later ones are often knock-on effects of it.
- The column points to where the compiler got confused, which is often just *after* the real mistake.

**Warnings** don't stop the build, but with `-Wall -Wextra` they flag code that's legal and almost certainly wrong. Treat them like errors.

steps.title: Reading an error
steps: `4:5` means line 4, column 5: the start of `cout`.
*Undeclared identifier* means the compiler doesn't know that name here.
The standard library puts its names in the namespace `std`, so the console is called `std::cout`. The compiler even suggests it.
steps.answer: Change line 4 to `std::cout << "Hi\n";`. Most first errors are this kind: a missing `std::`, a typo, or a missing `;`.

steps.prompt: This should print `Lives: 3`, but it doesn't build. Click the line with the mistake.
steps.error: error: expected ';' at end of declaration
fixes: Add `;` at the end of line 4: `int lives = 3;`
steps.explanation: Every statement ends with `;`, and line 4 is missing one: the error's column points at the end of that line. An extra `;` on line 3 is just an empty statement, and changing line 5 or the `#include` leaves line 4 broken, so all three still fail with the same error.

steps.prompt: Will the compiler catch it, or will it only show up when the program runs?
buckets: The compiler rejects it: no program is built
It builds: the problem shows up only when it runs

items.text: A missing `;` at the end of a statement
A loop that runs one time too many
Dividing by a number the player typed in, which happens to be 0
Printing "You win" when the player actually lost

steps.explanation: The compiler checks spelling, names, types and argument counts, so those never reach a running program: clang says *no member named 'cot' in namespace 'std'*, *cannot initialize a variable of type 'int' with an lvalue of type 'const char[5]'* and *no matching function for call to 'add'*. It can't know what the player will type or what you meant, so logic mistakes and bad run-time values still need testing.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.takeaway: Every variable has one fixed type, decided before the program runs; give each one a value when you declare it.

steps.title: Every variable has a type
steps.body:
```cpp
int lives = 3;            // whole numbers
double speed = 2.5;       // decimals
float scale = 0.5f;       // smaller, less precise decimals: note the f
bool alive = true;        // true or false
char grade = 'A';         // one character, in single quotes
std::string name = "Ada"; // text, in double quotes: #include <string>
```

A variable's type is fixed for its whole life. `lives = "three";` doesn't build: *assigning to 'int' from incompatible type 'const char[6]'*.

This is **static typing**: the compiler knows every type before the program runs. It catches mistakes early and lets the compiler produce fast machine code. Python, by contrast, checks types only as each line runs.

steps.title: auto, and text
steps.body:
`auto` asks the compiler to work out the type from the starting value. The variable is still statically typed:

```cpp
auto a = 7;      // int
auto b = 7.0;    // double
auto c = 2.5f;   // float
auto d = 'x';    // char
auto s = "hi";   // const char*, NOT std::string
```

That last one is a classic trap: a quoted literal is an old C-style array of characters, not a `std::string`. Write `std::string s = "hi";` when you want text you can join and change.

`std::string` basics: `+` joins strings, `s.size()` is the length, `s[0]` is the first `char`, and `std::to_string(42)` turns a number into text.

steps.prompt: Which type does `auto` deduce? Sort each declaration.
steps.explanation: A whole-number literal is an `int`, and anything with a decimal point or an exponent (`1e3`) is a `double`. `7 / 2` is int divided by int, so it stays an `int`; one `double` operand makes `7 / 2.0` a `double`. Single quotes make a `char`, and a comparison such as `3 > 2` gives a `bool`. (Each of these was checked with `static_assert`.)

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `std::to_string(7)` turns the number into the text `"7"`, so `tag` is `Ada#7`, which has 5 characters. `tag[0]` is the first character, the `char` `'A'`.

steps.title: Always initialise
steps.body:
A local `int`, `double`, `bool`, `char` or pointer declared without a value is **uninitialised**: it holds whatever bits were left in that memory. Reading it is **undefined behaviour** (UB): the C++ standard says nothing about what happens. The program may print garbage, print 0 today and 6 tomorrow, or change behaviour when optimised.

```cpp
int total;        // garbage
int count = 0;    // 0
int hits{};       // {} also means zero
std::string s;    // fine: strings and vectors start empty
```

The compiler won't stop you, but `-Wall` warns: *variable 'total' is uninitialized when used here*. Initialise every variable where you declare it.

steps.prompt: This should print `5`. On one run it printed `6`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
warning: variable 'coins' is uninitialized when used here [-Wuninitialized]
...
6
steps.hint: Which variable is read before anything was stored in it?
steps.explanation: `int coins;` leaves `coins` uninitialised, so `coins += found` adds 5 to whatever bits were there (on this run, 1). Giving it a starting value on line 4 fixes it. Zeroing `found` or adding a literal `5` still reads the garbage, and clang still warns. `auto` can't deduce a type from nothing: *declaration of variable 'coins' with deduced type 'auto' requires an initializer*.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: A `char` is a small integer. What type is `grade + 1`?
steps.explanation: `std::cout` prints a `bool` as `1` or `0` (send `std::boolalpha` first if you want `true`). A `char` prints as its letter, `A`. But `grade + 1` is arithmetic: the `char` is promoted to the `int` 65 (its character code), so it prints `66`. To get the letter `B`, convert back with `static_cast<char>(grade + 1)`.

lessons.title: Integer maths and overflow
lessons.takeaway: int divided by int is an int (`7 / 2` is 3), and every integer type has a limit: going past it with a signed type is undefined behaviour.

steps.title: Integer division
steps.body:
When both sides of `/` are integers, C++ does **integer division** and drops the fraction (it truncates toward zero): `7 / 2` is `3` and `-7 / 2` is `-3`. `%` gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`.

If either side is a `double`, you get real division: `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`.

The **operands** decide the type, not where you store the result: `double avg = 7 / 2;` computes the `int` 3 first and only then stores `3.0`. To divide two `int` variables properly, convert one of them first:

```cpp
double avg = static_cast<double>(total) / count;
```

`static_cast<T>(x)` is C++'s explicit conversion.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `7 / 2` is integer division, `3`; `7 % 2` is the remainder, `1`; `7 / 2.0` has a `double` operand, so it's `3.5`. On the next line `7 / 2` is still `3` before it's stored in `average`, and `std::cout` prints the `double` 3.0 as `3`.

steps.title: Hit accuracy
steps.problem: `int hits = 7; int shots = 8;` A programmer writes `double accuracy = hits / shots * 100;` and the HUD shows `0`. Work out why before revealing, then fix it.
steps: `hits / shots` is `int / int`, so 7 / 8 is `0`: the 0.875 is thrown away.
`0 * 100` is `0`, and storing it in a `double` just makes it `0.0`.
Convert before dividing: `static_cast<double>(hits) / shots * 100`. Now 7.0 / 8 is 0.875, and the result is 87.5.
steps.answer: `double accuracy = static_cast<double>(hits) / shots * 100;` gives `87.5`. Converting the result instead, as in `static_cast<double>(hits / shots)`, is too late: the fraction is already gone.

steps.prompt: This should print the average health, `83.3333`. It prints `83`. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 6 to `double average = static_cast<double>(total) / count;`
Change line 6 to `double average = static_cast<double>(total / count);`
Change line 6 to `auto average = total / count;`
steps.explanation: `total / count` divides two `int`s, so 250 / 3 is 83 before it's ever stored in the `double`. Converting `total` first makes it a `double` division. Converting the finished quotient, casting at print time or using `auto` (which deduces `int`) all keep the integer result `83`.

steps.title: Overflow
steps.body:
Each integer type has a fixed size. On every mainstream platform `int` is 32 bits, from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, and `long long` is 64 bits (up to about 9.2 × 10^18).

Going past the top is **overflow**, and the two kinds of integer behave differently:

- **Signed** types (`int`, `long long`): overflow is **undefined behaviour**. There's no promise that it wraps around, and the optimiser assumes it never happens.
- **Unsigned** types (`unsigned int`, and `std::size_t`, which `.size()` returns): arithmetic wraps around. For a 32-bit `unsigned int`, `0u - 1` is 4,294,967,295.

Give counters that keep growing, such as scores or milliseconds, a type with room to spare.

steps.prompt: A game stores the milliseconds since launch in an `int`. After how many days of running does it pass the `int` maximum, 2,147,483,647? Answer to one decimal place.
steps.hint: Divide by 1000 for seconds, then by 60, 60 and 24.
steps.explanation: 2,147,483,647 ms ÷ 1000 ÷ 60 ÷ 60 ÷ 24 ≈ **24.86 days**. A server or console left running for a month would hit it. The same mistake with an unsigned 32-bit counter wraps after about 49.7 days, a real bug that froze Windows 95 and 98 machines. A `long long` of milliseconds lasts about 292 million years.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Unsigned arithmetic wraps around. The largest 32-bit unsigned value is 4,294,967,295.
steps.explanation: `ammo` is unsigned, so `2 - 3` can't be -1. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2^32, landing on the largest value, `4294967295`. This is why code like `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector gives a huge number instead of -1.

steps.prompt: The score should go from 2147483000 up to `2147484000`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
-2147483296

Built with -fsanitize=undefined:
runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483000 + 1000 cannot be represented in type 'int'
steps.hint: What is the largest value an `int` can hold?
steps.explanation: The sum is bigger than the largest `int`, so `score += 1000` overflows: undefined behaviour, which on this machine came out as a large negative number. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (`-fsanitize=undefined`) reports it. A 64-bit `long long` has room. Rewriting the addition changes nothing, `auto` still deduces `int` from the literal, and casting when printing is too late: the overflow already happened.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.takeaway: `if`/`else if` runs the first true branch, loops repeat while a condition holds, and `==` compares while `=` assigns.

steps.title: if, else if, else
Loops

steps.prompt: Step through the loop and predict the values.

frames.note: `hp > 0` was true, so the body runs.
`turns` is 3. Back at line 3, `hp > 0` is now false, so the loop ends.

steps.hint: Each round subtracts 4. The loop only notices `hp` is no longer positive when it gets back to line 3.
steps.explanation: The condition is checked at the top of each round: 10 → 6 → 2 → -2 takes three rounds. Because the check only happens before a round, `hp` can end below zero. `hp <= 0` is then `true`.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `i = 1` is printed. `i = 2` is even, so `continue` skips the print. `i = 3` is printed. At `i = 4`, `4 % 4 == 0`, so `break` ends the loop before 5 to 10 ever run.

steps.title: Order matters in else-if
steps.problem: Label a hit: 50 or more is `"critical"`, 20 or more is `"heavy"`, anything else is `"light"`. A teammate wrote the `>= 20` check first. What does their version say for a hit of 60?
steps: The branches are tested top to bottom, and the first true one wins.
With `if (damage >= 20)` first, 60 passes that test, so it returns `"heavy"` and never reaches the `>= 50` check.
Put the strictest threshold first: `>= 50`, then `>= 20`, then `else`.

steps.prompt: With 3 lives this should print `Lives left: 3`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
warning: using the result of an assignment as a condition without parentheses [-Wparentheses]
...
Lives left: 0
steps.explanation: `lives = 0` **assigns** 0, and the condition's value is that 0, which counts as false. So the `else` branch runs and prints the lives that were just set to 0. `==` compares. Extra parentheses only silence clang's warning, `lives = 3` is always true and prints `Game over`, and starting at 0 lives changes the input, not the bug.
The inner loop starts at `j = i`: when `i` is 0 it runs for j = 0, 1, 2 (3 stars), when `i` is 1 for j = 1, 2 (2 stars), and when `i` is 2 once. 3 + 2 + 1 = **6**.

lessons.title: Functions and overloading
lessons.takeaway: A function declares its parameter and return types and must be declared before it's called; overloads share a name and differ in their parameters.

steps.title: Writing a function

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `greet("Bo")` prints `Hi Bo`. Then `square(3) + square(4)` is 9 + 16, so `25`.

steps.prompt: This should print `42`, but it doesn't build. Click the line the compiler complains about.
fixes: Add the declaration `int twice(int x);` above `main` (as a new line 2)
steps.explanation: The compiler reads top to bottom. On line 4 it hasn't seen `twice` yet, so the name is unknown. A declaration above `main` tells it the function exists, and the linker finds the definition later. `auto` or `void` on line 7 don't change the order (and `void` adds *void function 'twice' should not return a value*), and `twice` isn't part of the standard library: *no member named 'twice' in namespace 'std'*.

steps.title: Overloading and default arguments

steps.prompt: Two overloads of `show`. What does this print?
steps.hint: A `char` is a small integer. Converting it to `int` is a better match than converting it to `double`.
steps.explanation: `7 / 2` is an `int` (3), so `show(int)` runs. `7 / 2.0` is a `double` (3.5), so `show(double)` runs. `'A'` is a `char`: there's no `show(char)`, and promoting a `char` to `int` is a better match than converting it to `double`, so it prints its character code, `int 65`.

steps.title: Splitting out a function
steps.problem: Armour absorbs damage: a hit loses `armour` points, but it can never heal the target. Write `damageAfterArmour(damage, armour)`, and work out what it returns for (30, 12) and (5, 12) before revealing.
steps: Both inputs and the result are whole numbers, so the signature is `int damageAfterArmour(int damage, int armour)`.
Subtract first: `int result = damage - armour;`
Guard the edge case: if `result` is negative, return 0; otherwise return `result`.

steps.hint: Arguments fill the parameters from the left; anything left over uses its default.
steps.explanation: `dmg(5)` uses both defaults: 5 × 2 + 0 = 10. `dmg(5, 3)` overrides `mult`: 15. `dmg(5, 1, 4)` overrides both: 5 + 4 = 9. 10 + 15 + 9 = **34**. Arguments fill parameters left to right, so you can't skip `mult` and set only `bonus`.

units.title: Data and memory
units.description: References, vectors, maps and a first look at pointers.

lessons.title: References and const&
lessons.takeaway: Arguments are copied by default: take `T&` to change the caller's object and `const T&` to read a big object without copying it.

steps.title: Copies by default
steps.body:
Passing an argument **copies** it into the parameter, so changing the parameter changes only the copy:

```cpp
void healCopy(int hp) { hp += 10; }   // the caller's value is unchanged
```

A **reference**, written `int&`, is another name for an existing variable. No copy is made: every use of the reference *is* a use of the original.

```cpp
int gold = 100;
int& purse = gold;   // purse is another name for gold
purse -= 30;         // gold is now 70
```

A reference parameter, `void healRef(int& hp)`, lets a function change the caller's variable. A reference must be bound when it's created and always refers to the same object.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `healCopy` adds 10 to its own copy, which disappears when the function returns, so `a` is still `50`. clang even warns *parameter 'hp' set but not used*. `healRef` takes `a` by reference, so the `+= 10` lands on `a` itself: `60`.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict `gold` when asked.

frames.note: `purse` is another name for `gold`, not a new variable.
`copy` is a separate `int` that starts at 70.

steps.hint: A reference can never be re-seated: assigning to it assigns to the variable it names.
steps.explanation: Every change through `purse` is a change to `gold`, because they're the same variable: `purse -= 30` makes `gold` 70. `int copy = gold;` makes an independent copy, so `copy += 5` leaves `gold` alone. Finally `purse = copy` **assigns** 75 to `gold`; it doesn't make `purse` refer to `copy`.

steps.title: const& for reading big things
steps.body:
Copying an `int` is free, but copying a `std::vector` of 10,000 enemies or a long `std::string` means allocating and copying all of it, on every call. A **const reference** avoids the copy *and* promises not to change the original:

```cpp
int totalWeight(const std::vector<Item>& items);
```

If the function tries to modify it, the build fails: *cannot assign to variable 'score' with const-qualified type 'const int &'*.

Rules of thumb for parameters:
- small built-in types (`int`, `double`, `bool`, `char`): by value
- bigger objects you only read (`std::string`, `std::vector`, your own structs): `const T&`
- anything the function must change for the caller: `T&`

steps.prompt: Pick the parameter style for each function's argument.

items.text: A `double` speed used in a formula
A `char` for the key that was pressed
A `std::string` player name that is only printed
A large `Level` struct the function only reads
An `int` score the function must increase for the caller
A `std::vector<Item>` inventory the function adds an item to

steps.explanation: Small built-in values are cheaper to copy than to reach through a reference, so pass them by value. Anything bigger that's only read goes by `const T&`: no copy, and the compiler enforces read-only. When the caller must see the change, use a plain `T&`.

steps.prompt: `swapValues` should swap `x` and `y`, so this should print `2 1`. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 3 to `void swapValues(int& a, int& b) {`
Change line 3 to `void swapValues(const int& a, const int& b) {`
Change line 3 to `void swapValues(int& a, int b) {`
steps.hint: Which variables does `a = b;` change?
steps.explanation: `a` and `b` are copies, so the function swaps its own copies and throws them away. `int& a, int& b` make them names for the caller's `x` and `y`. `const int&` forbids the assignments (*cannot assign to variable 'a' with const-qualified type 'const int &'*), swapping the arguments in the call still swaps copies, and making only `a` a reference sets `x` to 2 but leaves `y` at 2: `2 2`.

lessons.title: Vectors, arrays and range-for
lessons.takeaway: `std::vector` is the default container, range-for visits its elements (`&` to change them), and `.at()` checks indexes where `[]` doesn't.

steps.title: std::vector
steps.body:
```cpp
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> hp = {30, 12, 7};
hp.push_back(5);      // add to the end: {30, 12, 7, 5}
hp.size();            // 4
hp[0];                // 30, the first element
hp.back();            // 5, the last element
hp.pop_back();        // remove the last element
hp.empty();           // false
```

A `std::vector<T>` is a growable array of `T`s stored side by side in memory. It's the container you'll use most, and games love it: the CPU reads memory that sits together fastest. The `<int>` fixes the element type: a vector holds one type only. Indexes start at 0, so the last valid one is `size() - 1`.

steps.title: Looping over a vector
steps.body:
```cpp
for (int x : hp) { ... }           // x is a copy of each element
for (int& x : hp) { x *= 2; }      // x is the element itself
for (const auto& e : enemies) {}   // read big elements without copying
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < hp.size(); ++i) { hp[i]; }   // when you need the index
```

The **range-for** loop visits every element in order. Its loop variable follows the rules from the last lesson: a plain type is a copy, `&` refers to the real element, and `const auto&` reads without copying.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Which loop changes the vector: the one with `int x` or the one with `int& x`?
steps.explanation: The first loop changes copies, so nothing happens (clang warns *variable 'x' set but not used*). The second loop's `int& x` is each real element, so the vector becomes 60, 24, 14. `push_back(1)` adds a fourth element, and the last loop prints all four followed by `size()`, 4.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict the vector when asked.
steps.explanation: `push_back` appends, so the vector grows to `[4, 9, 2]`. `v[0] = v[1] + v[2]` overwrites the first element with 9 + 2 = 11. `pop_back` removes the last element (the 2), leaving two, and `back()` reads the new last element, 9.

steps.title: `[]` vs `.at()`
steps.body:
`v[i]` doesn't check `i`. Reading past the end is **undefined behaviour**: you might get garbage, a crash, or a program that seems fine until it quietly corrupts something else.

`v.at(i)` checks, and throws `std::out_of_range` if `i` isn't between `0` and `size() - 1`, so the program stops with a clear message instead:

```
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::out_of_range: vector
```

Use `.at()` while learning and whenever an index comes from outside (player input, files). Engines use `[]` in hot loops for speed and catch mistakes in debug builds with **AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address`), which reports a *heap-buffer-overflow* at the bad line.

steps.prompt: This should print the total score, `19`. It crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::out_of_range: vector
fixes: Change line 7 to `for (std::size_t i = 0; i < scores.size(); ++i) {`
Change line 7 to `for (std::size_t i = 1; i <= scores.size(); ++i) {`
steps.hint: With 3 elements, which indexes are valid?
steps.explanation: With 3 scores the valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2, but `i <= scores.size()` also runs the body for `i = 3`, and `.at(3)` throws. Use `<`. Switching to `scores[i]` only hides the crash: on our run it even printed 19 by luck, but reading `scores[3]` is undefined behaviour, and AddressSanitizer reports *heap-buffer-overflow*. Starting at 1 skips the 7 and still reads index 3, and the type of `total` has nothing to do with it. (A range-for, `for (int s : scores)`, can't get the bounds wrong at all.)

steps.title: std::array for fixed sizes
steps.problem: A colour always has exactly three channels. Should it be a `std::vector<int>` or a `std::array<int, 3>`? Decide, then reveal.
steps: `std::array<T, N>` (`#include <array>`) has a size fixed when you compile: `std::array<int, 3> rgb = {255, 128, 0};`
It has no `push_back`: `rgb.push_back(7)` fails with *no member named 'push_back' in 'std::array<int, 3>'*.
It stores its elements directly, with no separate heap allocation, and supports `[]`, `.at()`, `.size()` and range-for just like a vector.
steps.answer: `std::array<int, 3>`: the count never changes. Use `std::vector` when the number of elements changes while the program runs.

steps.prompt: Vector or array?

items.text: Items the player has picked up
The x, y and z of a position
The four corners of a rectangle
The names of the seven days of the week

steps.explanation: If the count changes at run time (enemies spawn and die, messages arrive, items get picked up), use a `std::vector`. If the count is part of what the thing *is* (3 coordinates, 4 corners, 7 days), a `std::array` says so and needs no heap allocation.

lessons.title: Maps: lookup by key
lessons.takeaway: `std::unordered_map` finds a value by its key in about constant time, but `m[key]` inserts missing keys: check with `contains` and read with `at`.

steps.title: Lookup by key
The `[]` trap
steps.body:
`m[key]` never fails: if the key is missing, it **inserts** it with a default value (`0` for numbers, `""` for strings) and returns that. That's handy for counting, because `++counts[word];` starts every new word at 0.

But it's wrong for *checking*: asking `price["bow"]` quietly adds a bow to the shop. To check without changing the map, use `contains`; to read a key that must exist, use `at`.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `stock["pear"]` doesn't find a pear, so it inserts one with the value 0 and prints `0`. Now the map has 2 keys. `contains("kiwi")` only checks, and `std::cout` prints the `false` as `0`.

steps.title: Counting with a map
steps.problem: Count how often each enemy type appears in `{"orc", "elf", "orc", "imp", "orc"}`. Predict `counts["orc"]` and `counts.size()` before revealing.
steps: Start with an empty `std::unordered_map<std::string, int> counts;`.
For each word, `++counts[w];`. The first time a word appears, `[]` inserts it with 0 and `++` makes it 1.
After the loop: orc 3, elf 1, imp 1.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict the values. (The map is shown sorted by key; an `unordered_map`'s real order is unspecified.)

frames.note: A missing key is inserted as 0, then `+= 1` makes it 1.

steps.hint: Does `kills["troll"]` change the map?
steps.explanation: Each `kills[...] += 1` inserts the key at 0 the first time, so orc ends at 2 and elf at 1. Reading `kills["troll"]` returns 0, but it also **inserts** troll, so the map now has 3 keys.

steps.prompt: The shop sells 2 items. This should print `bow is not sold`, then `2 items for sale`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
bow is not sold
3 items for sale
steps.hint: What does `[]` do with a key that isn't in the map?
steps.explanation: `price[item]` can't find a bow, so it inserts one priced 0, and the shop now lists 3 items. `contains` checks without inserting. `at` throws for a missing key (*unordered_map::at: key not found*), `price[item] < 1` inserts just the same, and dropping the `!` reverses the test, so the message never prints.

steps.prompt: Pick the container for each job.

items.text: Health of each enemy, in spawn order
Scores to sort into a leaderboard
Item prices, looked up by item name
Settings looked up by key, such as "volume"
How many times each word appears in a chat log
The red, green and blue channels of a colour
The x and y of a 2D point

steps.explanation: Ordered sequences you append to or sort are vectors. When you find things by a key rather than a position, use a map. When the number of elements is fixed by what the thing is, use an array.

lessons.title: Pointers, briefly
lessons.takeaway: A pointer holds an address: `&` takes one, `*` follows it, and `nullptr` means it points nowhere, so check before you follow it.

steps.title: Addresses
steps.body:
Every variable lives somewhere in memory, at an **address**. `&x` gives that address, and a **pointer** stores one:

```cpp
int a = 5;
int* p = &a;    // p holds the address of a
*p = 6;         // * follows the pointer: a is now 6
```

`int*` reads "pointer to int". Unlike a reference, a pointer can be changed to point somewhere else, and it can point **nowhere**: `nullptr`. Following a null pointer is undefined behaviour, usually a crash, so check first: `if (p != nullptr)`.

Printing `p` itself shows a raw address that changes from run to run, which is why the trace below shows `&a` instead.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict the values.

frames.note: `p` holds the address of `a`, so `*p` reads `a`.
`p` now points nowhere: `*p` would be undefined behaviour.

steps.hint: `*p` is whatever variable `p` currently points at.
steps.explanation: `*p += 1` writes through the pointer into `a`, making it 6. `p = &b` changes the **pointer**, not any `int`: now `*p` reads `b`, which is 8. `*p = *p * 2` doubles `b` to 16 and leaves `a` alone.

steps.title: `->`, and when to use pointers
steps.body:
For a pointer to a struct or class, `p->hp` is shorthand for `(*p).hp`:

```cpp
Player hero;
Player* p = &hero;
p->hp -= 25;   // same as (*p).hp -= 25
```

Prefer a **reference** when something must always exist. Use a pointer when it may be missing (`nullptr`) or must be re-pointed later, like a turret's current target.

A pointer to something that has been destroyed is **dangling**: it still holds the old address, and using it is undefined behaviour. Pointers that *own* memory are a separate story, coming in the heap lesson.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `p` and `r` both reach `score`: `*p = 20` sets it to 20 and `r = r + 5` makes it 25, so `score` and `*p` are both `25`. A reference has no address of its own, so `&r` is the address of `score`, the same as `p`: the comparison is true, printed as `1`.

steps.prompt: This should print the first negative value, or print nothing if there isn't one. It crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Built with -fsanitize=address,undefined:
runtime error: load of null pointer of type 'int'
...
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000
steps.hint: What does `findFirstNegative` return for `{30, 12, 7}`?
steps.explanation: No value is negative, so `findFirstNegative` returns `nullptr`, and `*hit` follows a null pointer: undefined behaviour, here a segmentation fault. Check before dereferencing. Printing `hit` itself prints the pointer (`0`), not nothing. `return 0;` is just another way to write a null pointer, so it crashes the same way, and `&findFirstNegative(hp)` doesn't build: *cannot take the address of an rvalue of type 'int *'*.

steps.prompt: Reference or pointer?

items.text: Must be bound to an object when it's created
Every use is automatically a use of the original, no `*` needed
A parameter that must always refer to a real player
Can be re-pointed at another object later
A turret's current target, which may be nobody

steps.explanation: A reference is a permanent second name: always bound, never null, never re-pointed, so it's the natural choice when something must exist. A pointer is a value holding an address: it can be null or change, which suits optional or changing relationships, and it needs `*` or `->` to reach the object.

units.title: Your own types
units.description: Structs and classes, enum class, std::optional and splitting code into files.

lessons.title: Structs and classes
lessons.takeaway: A struct or class bundles data with the member functions that use it; private members plus public functions keep its rules true, and objects copy like values.

steps.title: Grouping data with struct

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `Vec2 b = a;` copies `a`, so setting `b.x` to 10 leaves `a.x` at 1. `c` is created without arguments, so its members take their default values: `c.y` is `0`.

steps.title: Classes protect their rules

steps.prompt: Using the `Player` class above, predict `kai.hp()` when asked.
steps.hint: `heal` never goes above `maxHp_`, and `takeDamage` never goes below 0.
steps.explanation: `heal(50)` would reach 120, but `std::min(maxHp_, ...)` caps it at 100. Taking 45 leaves 55, and taking 200 would go negative, so `std::max(0, ...)` stops at 0. Healing 15 from 0 gives 15. The rules live in two member functions, and nothing outside the class can bypass them.

steps.prompt: This should add 25 more coins and print `75`, but it doesn't build. Click the line with the error.
steps.error: error: 'coins_' is a private member of 'Wallet'
fixes: Change line 5 to `void deposit(int amount) const {`
steps.hint: Which members can code outside the class use?
steps.explanation: `coins_` is private, so only `Wallet`'s own member functions may touch it. Go through the public interface: `w.deposit(25)`. `w.coins()` returns a copy of the number, which can't be assigned to (*expression is not assignable*). `Wallet::coins_` is still private and names no particular wallet, and making `deposit` `const` forbids it from changing `coins_` at all.

steps.prompt: A C# programmer asks what really differs between `struct` and `class` in C++. What's the answer?
choices: Only the default access: members are public in a `struct` and private in a `class`
A `struct` is copied on assignment, while a `class` object is shared by reference
A `struct` can't have constructors or member functions
`class` objects always live on the heap, and `struct` objects on the stack
steps.explanation: In C++ the two keywords make the same kind of type. Both copy on assignment, both can have constructors and member functions, and either can live on the stack or the heap. The only difference is the default access, so by convention `struct` is used for plain data and `class` for types with rules to protect.

lessons.title: enum class and std::optional
lessons.takeaway: `enum class` gives a fixed set of named states that a `switch` can handle, and `std::optional<T>` says "a T, or nothing" without magic values.

steps.title: enum class and switch

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Which case has no `break`?
steps.explanation: `Weapon::Sword` has no `break`, so after `d += 10` execution falls through into the `Bow` case and adds 5 more: `15`. `Bow` gives `5` and `Staff` gives `1`. A missing `break` is a classic bug; when you really want to fall through, write `[[fallthrough]];` to say so.

steps.prompt: This should print `facing right`, but it doesn't build. Click the line with the error.
steps.error: error: invalid operands to binary expression ('Dir' and 'int')
steps.explanation: An `enum class` never converts to `int`, so `facing == 1` has no meaning. Compare with a value of the same type: `Dir::Right`. The names are scoped, so plain `Right` is an *undeclared identifier*; `=` assigns, and a `Dir` *is not contextually convertible to 'bool'*; and a string literal isn't a `Dir` either.

steps.title: std::optional
Where is the key?
steps.problem: Write `findItem(bag, name)`, which returns the slot an item is in, or nothing. What should it return, and how does the caller use the result? Decide before revealing.
steps: The result is either an index or nothing, so the return type is `std::optional<std::size_t>`.
Loop over the slots and `return i;` on a match (it converts to an optional holding `i`). After the loop, `return std::nullopt;`.
The caller can test it right in the `if`: `if (auto slot = findItem(bag, "key"))`, then use `*slot` inside.

steps.prompt: Using `parseLevel` from above, what does this print?
steps.explanation: `"hard"` gives an optional holding 3, so `value_or(0)` returns `3`. `"nightmare"` matches nothing, so `b` is empty: `value_or(0)` falls back to `0`, and `has_value()` is false, printed as `0`.

steps.prompt: With no scores yet this should print `Best: 0`. It crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::bad_optional_access: bad_optional_access
steps.hint: What does `best` return for an empty vector, and what does `.value()` do with that?
steps.explanation: `best` correctly returns an empty optional for an empty vector, but `.value()` on an empty optional throws `std::bad_optional_access`. `value_or(0)` supplies the fallback. `return {};` is just another way to write `std::nullopt`, an optional can't be printed directly (*invalid operands to binary expression*), and `= {}` still makes an empty vector.

lessons.title: Headers and source files
lessons.takeaway: Headers declare what exists and `.cpp` files define how it works; each `.cpp` compiles on its own and the linker joins them.

steps.title: Splitting a program into files

steps.prompt: Put what happens when you run `clang++ main.cpp math.cpp -o game` in order.
items: The contents of `math.h` are pasted into each `.cpp` file that includes it
`main.cpp` and `math.cpp` are compiled separately into two object files
The linker matches the call to `add` in one object file with its definition in the other
steps.explanation: Including happens first, as plain text pasting. Then each `.cpp` file is compiled on its own: while compiling `main.cpp`, the compiler only knows `add` from its declaration. Joining the call to the actual function body is the linker's job, and only then is there a program to run.

steps.title: Linker errors
steps.body:
A **compiler** error names a file and line. A **linker** error comes later, after every file compiled fine, when the pieces don't fit together:

- Something is declared and called but never defined, or its `.cpp` file was left out of the build:

```
Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
  "add(int, int)", referenced from:
      _main in main-c7f57c.o
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64
```

- Something is **defined** in a header that two `.cpp` files include, so it now exists twice: *duplicate symbol*.

Rule of thumb: headers hold declarations, class definitions and templates. Function bodies go in `.cpp` files, written as `void Player::takeDamage(int amount) { ... }` for member functions, or are marked `inline`.

steps.prompt: Three files are shown together. `clang++ hud.cpp main.cpp -o game` should build a program that prints `30`, but linking fails. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
duplicate symbol 'bonus(int)' in:
    .../hud-5f71e5.o
    .../main-f7fbeb.o
ld: 1 duplicate symbols
fixes: Change line 4 to `inline int bonus(int level) {`
steps.hint: How many object files end up containing the body of `bonus`?
steps.explanation: `#pragma once` only prevents a double paste *within one file*. Both `hud.cpp` and `main.cpp` include the header, so both object files contain a full definition of `bonus`, and the linker refuses to pick one. `inline` allows identical definitions in several files (the other fix is to leave only the declaration in the header and move the body to a `score.cpp`). Removing `#pragma once` changes nothing here, angle brackets don't search the current folder (*'score.h' file not found with <angled> include*), and without the include `hud.cpp` doesn't know `bonus` at all.

steps.prompt: Header or source file?

items.text: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`

steps.explanation: Headers say *what exists*: declarations and type definitions that every file using them needs to see. Source files say *how it works*: function bodies, which must exist exactly once in the whole program, and `main`.

steps.prompt: The build stops with `Undefined symbols` for `"takeDamage(int)"`, and no file or line number. What's the most likely cause?
choices: `takeDamage` was declared and called, but its definition never made it into the build
`takeDamage` was called with a `double` instead of an `int`
steps.explanation: *Undefined symbols* is a linker error: every file compiled, but no object file contains the function's body. Maybe it was never written, or its `.cpp` file was left out of the compile command. A syntax error or a missing include are compiler errors with a file and line (a missing declaration gives *use of undeclared identifier*), and a `double` argument simply converts to `int`.

units.title: The modern toolkit
units.description: Lambdas and algorithms, owning heap memory with unique_ptr, and templates.

lessons.title: Lambdas and <algorithm>
lessons.takeaway: A lambda is an inline function whose `[]` says which local variables it captures; pass lambdas to `std::sort`, `std::count_if` and `std::find_if` instead of writing the loops.

steps.title: Lambdas
steps.body:
A **lambda** is a small function written right where you need it:

```cpp
auto twice = [](int x) { return x * 2; };
twice(4);   // 8
```

The `[]` is the **capture list**: the local variables from the surrounding code that the lambda may use.

- `[limit]` copies `limit` into the lambda when the lambda is created
- `[&total]` refers to `total` itself, so the lambda sees, and can change, its current value
- `[=]` copies everything the lambda uses; `[&]` refers to everything it uses

Using an ordinary local variable that isn't captured is a compile error.

steps.title: <algorithm>

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: The comparison lambda returns `a > b`, so bigger values go first: `75, 40, 20, 5`. `hp[0]` is `75` and `hp[3]` is `5`. `count_if` counts the elements for which the lambda returns true: 20 and 5 are below 30, so `2`.

steps.title: Finding an enemy
steps.problem: Find the first enemy with less than 10 hp in `{{"orc", 40}, {"imp", 8}, {"elf", 3}}` and print its name. Which enemy is it, and what must you check before using the result?
steps: `std::find_if` with the lambda `[](const Enemy& e) { return e.hp < 10; }` walks the vector from the front.
The orc fails the test; the imp passes, so `find_if` stops there and returns an iterator to it. The elf also matches, but it's never reached.
If nothing matched, the iterator would equal `enemies.end()`, and using it would be undefined behaviour. Check first, then read the name with `it->name`.

steps.prompt: Two lambdas capture `bonus` in different ways. Predict the values when asked.

frames.note: `byValue` stored its own copy of `bonus` (5) when it was created.

steps.hint: A capture by value is taken once, when the lambda is created.
steps.explanation: `[bonus]` copied the value 5 when `byValue` was created, so later changes to `bonus` don't affect it: `byValue(1)` is 6. `[&bonus]` refers to the variable itself, so `byRef` sees the new 100: `byRef(1)` is 101.

steps.prompt: This should count the enemies below `limit` and print `2`, but it doesn't build. Click the line with the error.
steps.error: error: variable 'limit' cannot be implicitly captured in a lambda with no capture-default specified
fixes: On line 8, change the lambda to `[limit](int h) { return h < limit; }`
On line 8, change the lambda to `[](int h, int limit) { return h < limit; }`
On line 8, change the lambda to `[h](int h) { return h < limit; }`
On line 8, pass `limit` as an extra argument: `std::count_if(hp.begin(), hp.end(), [](int h) { return h < limit; }, limit)`
steps.explanation: `limit` is a local variable of `main`, and the lambda's empty `[]` doesn't capture it. `[limit]` copies it in. A second parameter doesn't work because `count_if` calls the lambda with one argument, `[h]` tries to capture a variable that doesn't exist (*use of undeclared identifier 'h'*), and `count_if` takes no fourth argument (*no matching function for call to 'count_if'*).

steps.hint: `it - v.begin()` is the index of the element `it` points at.
steps.explanation: `find_if` stops at the first element greater than 10. 8 and 3 fail; 15 at index 2 is the first match. `it - v.begin()` is the distance from the start: **2**.

lessons.title: The heap, new/delete and unique_ptr
lessons.takeaway: Locals die at the end of their scope; for heap objects use `std::make_unique`, whose owner frees them automatically on every path (RAII), and never write `delete` yourself.

steps.title: Stack and heap
steps.body:
Local variables live on the **stack**. Each is created when its line runs and destroyed automatically at the closing brace of its scope, in reverse order of creation. A class can run code at that moment in its **destructor**, written `~Name()`.

Sometimes an object must outlive the function that creates it, or how many you need is only known while the program runs. Then it goes on the **heap**:

```cpp
Enemy* e = new Enemy();   // allocate on the heap; you get a pointer
// ...
delete e;                 // you must free it yourself
```

C++ has no garbage collector. Every `new` needs exactly one `delete`: forget it and the memory **leaks**; delete twice, or use the object after `delete`, and it's undefined behaviour. (`std::vector` and `std::string` use the heap too, but free it themselves in their destructors.)

steps.prompt: The constructor prints `+name` and the destructor prints `-name`. What does this program print?
steps.hint: Objects are destroyed at the closing brace of their scope, newest first.
steps.explanation: `a` is created, then the inner braces create `b` and `c`. At the inner closing brace they're destroyed in reverse order: `-c -b`. Then `d` is created, and at the end of `main` the remaining objects are destroyed in reverse order: `-d -a`.

steps.prompt: `draw(false)` should load the texture and free it again, printing `load` then `free`. Click the line where the texture escapes.
fixes: Change line 10 to `auto t = std::make_unique<Texture>();` and delete line 14
Change line 14 to `delete t; delete t;`
Change line 10 to `Texture t = new Texture();`
Change line 12 to `return false; delete t;`
steps.hint: Follow `draw(false)` line by line. Which line leaves the function, and what does it skip?
steps.explanation: When `visible` is false, the early `return` on line 12 skips the `delete`, so the texture is never freed: a leak. Every new exit path would need its own `delete`. A `std::unique_ptr` frees the texture on every path out of `draw`. A second `delete` is never reached (and would be a double free if it were), code after `return` never runs, and a `Texture` isn't a `Texture*`: *no viable conversion from 'Texture *' to 'Texture'*.

steps.title: unique_ptr: the heap without delete
steps.body:
`std::unique_ptr<T>` (`#include <memory>`) is a small object that **owns** a heap object and deletes it in its own destructor:

```cpp
{
    auto t = std::make_unique<Enemy>();   // new, wrapped
    t->draw();                            // use it like a pointer
}                                         // t's scope ends: the Enemy is deleted
```

Because `t` itself is a local, it's destroyed on **every** way out of the scope (the normal end, an early `return`, an exception), so the object can't leak. Tying a resource to an object's lifetime like this is called **RAII** (resource acquisition is initialisation). It's how C++ manages memory, files and locks.

There's exactly one owner, so copying fails: *call to implicitly-deleted copy constructor of 'unique_ptr<int>'*. Handing ownership on with `std::move` comes later in the track. In modern C++, write `make_unique` instead of `new`, and never write `delete` yourself.

steps.prompt: The destructor prints `free` and the name. What does this print?
steps.output:
drawing
free tmp
end
free hero
steps.explanation: `tmp` is owned by a `unique_ptr` declared inside the inner braces, so it's freed right after `drawing`, at that closing brace. `hero`'s owner lives until the end of `main`, so it's freed after `end`. No `delete` anywhere, and nothing leaks.

steps.prompt: Who frees it?

items.text: A `Player` declared as a local variable
An object from `new Enemy()` stored in an `Enemy*`
The `Enemy*` returned by a function that called `new`

steps.explanation: Locals die at the end of their scope, and owners such as `unique_ptr` and `std::vector` free their heap memory in their destructors. Only a raw `new` leaves the job to you, which is why modern C++ code avoids it.

steps.prompt: Why is `auto t = std::make_unique<Texture>();` better than `Texture* t = new Texture();` with a `delete t;` at the end of the function?
choices: The texture is freed on every path out of the scope, including early returns and exceptions
It switches on a garbage collector for that object
Several owners can share the texture, and it's freed when the last one is done
The texture is stored on the stack, which is faster
steps.explanation: The `unique_ptr` is a local, so its destructor runs however the scope is left, and it deletes the texture. There's no garbage collector involved. Shared ownership is `std::shared_ptr`, a different tool. And the texture itself is still on the heap: only the small owner object is on the stack.

lessons.title: Templates: code for any type
lessons.takeaway: A template is a recipe the compiler turns into real code for each type you use it with; `std::vector<int>` and friends are templates too.

steps.title: One function for many types
steps.body:
```cpp
template <typename T>
T biggest(T a, T b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;   // condition ? if-true : if-false
}
```

```cpp
biggest(3, 7);              // T is int: 7
biggest(2.5, 9.0);          // T is double: 9
biggest<double>(2, 2.5);    // T named explicitly: 2.5
```

A **function template** is a recipe. When you call it, the compiler **deduces** `T` from the arguments and generates a real function for that type, at compile time. Any type works as long as the body compiles for it: here, `T` needs a `>`.

You've been using templates all along: `std::vector<int>`, `std::array<int, 3>`, `std::unordered_map<std::string, int>`, `std::optional<int>` and `std::unique_ptr<Texture>` are **class templates**, and the `<...>` are their template arguments.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `biggest(3, 7)` makes an `int` version and returns 7. `biggest(2.5, 9.0)` makes a `double` version and returns 9.0, printed as `9`. With `<std::string>` both literals become strings, which compare alphabetically, and "pear" comes after "apple": `pear`.

steps.prompt: What does `T` become in each call to `biggest`?
steps.explanation: Without `<...>`, `T` is the type of the arguments, and both must agree: `10 / 4` is an `int`, `10 / 4.0` a `double`, `'x'` a `char`. With `<...>`, you choose `T` and the arguments are converted to it. (Each answer was checked with `static_assert`.)

steps.prompt: This should print the bigger number, `2.5`, but it doesn't build. Click the line with the error.
steps.error:
error: no matching function for call to 'biggest'
note: candidate template ignored: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' vs. 'double')
fixes: Change line 4 to `int biggest(T a, T b) {`
Change line 3 to `template <typename T, typename T>`
steps.hint: What type does `2` suggest for `T`? And `2.5`?
steps.explanation: From `2` the compiler deduces `T = int` and from `2.5` it deduces `T = double`, and one `T` can't be both. Naming `T` as `double` converts the 2. `biggest<int>` builds but turns 2.5 into 2 (clang warns *implicit conversion from 'double' to 'int' changes value from 2.5 to 2*) and prints `2`. Changing the return type doesn't touch the deduction, and a template can't have two parameters with the same name.

steps.title: The text trap
steps.problem: `biggest("pear", "apple")` compiles. Why can't you trust its answer? Think it through, then reveal.
steps: Quoted literals aren't `std::string`s. Passed by value, they turn into `const char*`, so `T` is deduced as `const char*`.
`a > b` then compares two **addresses**, not the letters. Which literal sits at the higher address is up to the compiler.
Ask for real strings instead: `biggest<std::string>("pear", "apple")` returns `"pear"`.
steps.answer: With `T = const char*` the template compiles but compares pointers. Name the type, or pass `std::string`s, whenever a template gets text.

steps.prompt: When is the `double` version of `biggest` created?
choices: At compile time, because some call in the program needs `biggest<double>`
At run time, the first time the program calls it with doubles
Never: one shared version handles every type, as with Java generics
steps.explanation: The compiler generates a separate, fully typed function for each `T` the program uses, while it compiles. That's why templates cost nothing at run time, and why their errors appear at compile time. Java generics work differently: one compiled version works on `Object` references (type erasure).
